item.title: Statent 2024: 5.68 million jobs in Switzerland
item.description: In 2024, Switzerland recorded 5.68 million jobs, with a growth of 0.6% compared to the previous year according to the UST.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - 5.68 million jobs in 2024 - Growth of 0.6% compared to 2023 - 810,000 jobs created since 2011
## Key facts - **What**: Structural statistics of STATENT companies - When: 20 August 2026 - Where: Neuchâtel and all of Switzerland - Who: Federal Statistical Office UST - Amount: 810,000 jobs
On 20 August 2026, the Federal Statistical Office UST published the updated data relating to the structural business statistics statent, providing a detailed picture of the trend in employment and the national economic fabric. During 2024, the Swiss economy accounted for about 5.68 million jobs, registering a growth of 0.6% compared to the previous year. This positive percentage change represents the second lowest recorded since 2011, confirming a slowdown in overall employment dynamics. Looking at the period between 2011 and 2024, a total of over 810,000 jobs were created in Switzerland, a significant achievement driven almost entirely by the tertiary sector.
### Business sector analysis In 2024, just over 78% of the 649,000 companies surveyed in Switzerland carried out their main activity in the tertiary sector, focused on services. At the same time, the secondary sector, which includes industry, arts and crafts, accounted for just over 14% of total enterprises. Immediately after were the other service activities with 9.2% and agriculture, forestry and fisheries with 7.6%. From a purely employment point of view, the branches with the highest number of employees were public administration with 8.7% of total jobs, health services activities with 8.5% and retail trade with 5.9%.

item.title: Over 65s outnumber under 20s: the Swiss demographic turnaround
item.description: Over 65s (1.811 million) exceed the under 20s (1.804 million) in Switzerland for the first time. Population grows by 0.8%, with strong implications on AVS, LPP and sick pay.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - For the first time over 65 are over 20 in Switzerland - Population grows by 0.8% in 2025, slower than 2024 (1.0%) - Births falling but at a slower rate than in 2024 and 2023 - Net immigration remains positive at +70,400 people
## Key facts - **When**: 2025 (final UST data, just published) - Where: Switzerland (9,127,100 permanent residents) - Who: Federal Statistical Office (FSO) - Demographic inversion: 1.811 million over 65 vs 1.804 million under 20 - Population growth: 0.8% per year (slowdown vs 1.0% in 2024) - Migration balance: +70,400 people (-14.9% vs 2024)
For the first time in Swiss demographic history, the number of residents over the age of 65 has surpassed that of young people under the age of 20. This is confirmed by the final data of the Federal Statistical Office (FSO), just released, relating to the demographic trend of 2025. A historical scan that shows the progressive ageing of the Swiss population, with significant consequences for the social security system, the labour market and the national public finances.
The over-65s reached 1.811 million people, while the under-20s stood at 1.804 million. With more older and fewer young people active in the labour market, the pressure on AVS (old-age insurance) and LPP (occupational pension) contributions will increase significantly.
Currently, every active resident between the ages of 20 and 64 supports an increasing number of retirees through salary contributions. In 2025, the dependency ratio for the elderly stood at 32.8 inactive per 100 people of working age — for the first time higher than the youth dependency ratio (32.7). It means that the financial burden of the elderly pension has surpassed that of the generational pension. item.title: Demographic slowdown in 2025: +0.8%
item.description: As of December 31, 2025, Switzerland has 9.127 million inhabitants. Growth slows to 0.8%, the elderly outnumber the young for the first time. Implications on AVS, LPP and welfare.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Population 9,127 million at 31/12/2025: growth +0.8% (slowdown vs 1.0% 2024) - Elderly (65+) outnumber young people (<20) for the first time: 1,810,600 vs 1,804,500 - Migration balance falls by 14.9%; internal mobility falls (56 vs 61 displacements per 1,000 inhabitants) - Migration down 3.9%, emigration up 3.1% compared to 2024
## Key facts - **What**: Definitive demographic data 2025 from the Federal Statistical Office - When: 31 December 2025 (press release 20 August 2026) - Where: Switzerland, all 26 cantons - Who: UST (Federal Statistical Office) - Inhabitants: 9,127,100 (+0.8% per year) - Elderly (65+): 1,810,600 (outnumber young people <20 for the first time) - Migration balance: 70,400 (-14.9% compared to 2024)
Switzerland closes 2025 with 9,127,100 permanent residents. According to the final data of the Federal Statistical Office (FSO), population growth continues but at a significantly slower pace: +0.8% compared to 2024 (+1.0%) and 2023 (+1.7%). This slowdown reflects a year characterized by less immigration and more emigration, confirming the trends observed in the provisional data released in April 2026.
The profile of the population is transformed. Among the 9,127 million inhabitants, 6,599,000 have Swiss nationality (72%), while 2,528,100 are foreigners (28%). In 2025, the Swiss population grew by 27,900 people (+0.4%), while the foreign population increased by 48,200 people (+1.9%). ### Internal mobility on the decline Alongside comprehensive demographic data, the UST has provided information on population mobility within the Swiss territory. In 2025, 511,200 internal migrations were recorded: 358,000 intracantonal (within the same canton) and 153,200 intercantonal (between different cantons). When related to the number of inhabitants, these numbers highlight a trend of slowdown: only 56 movements per 1,000 inhabitants in 2025, compared to 61 per 1,000 inhabitants ten years earlier. This decline in internal mobility affects both nationality groups, albeit in different ways. In 2025, foreign people maintain a higher mobility compared to Swiss citizens (80 movements per 1,000 foreigners, against 47 per 1,000 Swiss citizens). However, it is precisely among Swiss citizens that the decline in mobility is more marked from 2021 onwards, suggesting growing residential stability or possible economic constraints related to housing costs. ### Pension system under pressure The UST's demographic data has direct repercussions on the sustainability of the Swiss pension system. When the elderly surpass the young, the ratio between active contributors and pensioners narrows, exerting financial pressure on AVS (Old Age Insurance) and LPP (Professional Pension). The natural population growth (only 8% of total growth in 2025) suggests that Switzerland will still rely on migratory balance for many years to maintain an adequate number of active workers. However, the decline in migratory balance in 2025 (-14.9%) indicates that this source of supply is weakening. At the territorial level, the 17 cantons with an older population will face more consistent welfare, health, and long-term care needs, while the nine cantons with younger demographic profiles can count on a broader contributory base. Consult our tools to verify your pension position. The variability between cantons suggests that demographic pressures are not uniform: Vaud, Geneva, Fribourg, and Zurich still maintain younger profiles, while other regions will face more acute sustainability challenges. ### Nationality and labor market dynamics The decline in immigration (-3.9% compared to 2024) and the increase in emigration (+3.1%) indicate changes in the attractive forces of the Swiss labor market. Among new immigrants, Germans remain the largest group (12.9% of flows), followed by Swiss returnees (11.3%), French (10.1%), and Italians (9.1%). On the other hand, Swiss emigration (22% of those leaving the country) suggests a search for opportunities abroad, while that of Portuguese, Italians, and French may reflect economic changes in their countries of origin. These migratory flows have direct effects on the Swiss labor market: fewer immigrants mean less labor supply for certain sectors (construction, hospitality, healthcare), but also less pressure on Swiss citizens' salaries, at least in the short term. [Check the cost of living and job opportunities in your region](nav:cost-of-living) to evaluate your position.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Planning for retirement in a context of aging The demographic implications presented by the UST data have a direct relevance for those planning their own retirement. With a growing life expectancy and an increasingly unfavorable ratio between active and pensioners, it is essential not to rely solely on the AVS guarantee. The contribution rates for the second pillar (LPP) vary by age group: from 7% between 25 and 34 years, to 10% between 35 and 44 years, to 15% between 45 and 54 years, up to 18% after 55 years up to the reference age. This means that the last years of career require a significantly higher contribution effort.
Anyone in one of the higher age groups should check if their LPP rate is correct and if the accumulated capital is sufficient. It is equally important to evaluate the opening of a third pillar account (3a) to integrate the obligatory pension. These tools allow for federal and cantonal tax deductions, reducing the tax burden while accumulating additional capital for retirement.
### Cost of living and housing dynamics The slowdown in demographic growth does not necessarily mean a decline in the cost of living in Switzerland. Rather, aging of the population implies a reconfiguration of housing demand: fewer expanding family units, more pensioners seeking housing solutions tailored to their needs. This phenomenon is reflected in property prices and rents at the local level, with marked variations between cantons. The cantons with the youngest population (Vaud, Geneva, Fribourg, Zurich) are likely to continue exerting pressure on prices, while those with more elderly populations may see emerging housing opportunities at a lower price.
For those living and working in Switzerland, monitoring local cost of living, LAMal premiums (obligatory health insurance), and cantonal taxes remains essential. The older cantons may be pushed to increase taxes to finance welfare, while the younger ones may be able to maintain a more competitive tax system.
### Labor mobility and contractual opportunities The observed decline in internal mobility (56 moves per 1,000 inhabitants in 2025, compared to 61 ten years ago) suggests that workers remain more stable in their places of residence. This trend may reflect a greater difficulty in finding accessible housing in other regions, or a greater preference for telework and flexibility. For employers, it means that the local pool of competitive talent is reduced, prompting them to invest more in internal training and job attractiveness.
Those looking for work in Switzerland should take advantage of this trend: the relative scarcity of mobile candidates amplifies personal bargaining power. It is advisable to negotiate flexibility in working hours, telework, performance bonuses, and salary supplements. Similarly, those already employed may find more favorable conditions in a job change, thanks to the sustained demand for talent in a context of general reduced mobility.

item.content:encoded:
## In Brief - Watch exports increase by 10% in July - 9.6% growth on an annual basis - United States is the main market - Exports valued at 2.63 billion francs
## Key Facts - **What**: Watch export trend - When: July - Where: Bienne (BE) - Who: Swiss Watch Industry Federation (FH) - Amount: 2.63 billion francs - Percentage: 10%
The Swiss watch industry has seen a significant increase in exports in July, with a 10% rise compared to the same period last year. This growth is largely driven by the strong demand in the United States, which remains the main market for Swiss watches. The total value of exports reached 2.63 billion francs, a 9.6% increase on an annual basis. The Swiss Watch Industry Federation (FH) has reported that the growth in exports is a positive sign for the industry, which has been affected by the global economic downturn. The FH has also noted that the growth in exports is a result of the strong demand in the United States, as well as in other key markets such as France and the United Kingdom. However, the industry is also facing challenges in other regions, such as Japan, where exports have declined.
The Swiss watch industry is a significant contributor to the country's economy, and the growth in exports is a positive sign for the industry. However, the industry is also facing challenges in other regions, and the FH has noted that the growth in exports is a result of the strong demand in the United States and other key markets. The industry is also closely monitoring the developments in the global economy and is adapting to the changing market conditions.
### Market Situation in Key Export Markets
The Swiss watch industry is heavily reliant on exports, and the growth in exports is a key driver of the industry's growth. The industry is closely monitoring the developments in the key export markets, including the United States, France, the United Kingdom, and Japan. The FH has reported that the growth in exports in these markets is a positive sign for the industry, and the industry is adapting to the changing market conditions.
A decisive factor in determining the trend of the industry is the development in the main export market, the United States. In July, exports to the US increased by 26.5%, following a 12.7% increase in June. Exports to France more than doubled, with a 104.6% increase, making France the second most important market. The UK, the fourth most important market, saw a 9.5% increase in exports. In contrast, Japan, the third most important market, saw a 3.7% decline in exports. These data highlight a polarization of international demand, with some European and North American markets showing exceptional performance, while other Asian markets show signs of contraction or slowdown. The ability of the Swiss watch industry to intercept foreign demand is confirmed as a fundamental pillar for the balance of the national trade balance. The analysis of disaggregated data by price range offers further insights into the Swiss watch industry's performance. The high-end segment, which includes watches priced at 3,000 francs or more, recorded a 12.0% increase in July. At the same time, the economic segment, characterized by watches priced between 200 and 500 francs, also registered a significant growth of 26.1%. According to the Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry (FH), it is precisely the more affordable watches that confirm the recovery of this year, after the same segment had recorded a consistent decline for four consecutive years. This polarization demonstrates how demand is moving simultaneously towards extreme luxury goods and more accessible products, partially excluding intermediate segments from such marked growth dynamics. The evolution of export volumes and values reflects different commercial strategies adopted by major groups and independent brands, engaged in positioning their catalogs based on the changing preferences of global consumers. item.title: Swiss exports accelerate in July 2026
item.description: In July 2026, Swiss exports reached CHF 27.8 billion (+13.8% monthly). The pharmaceutical sector is growing by 25%. Surplus trade balance: CHF 8.1 billion.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Swiss exports +13.8% in July 2026, maximum level since March 2025 - Trade balance surplus: new monthly record of CHF 8.1 billion - Pharmaceutical sector accelerates with +25% (+3.3 billion CHF)
## Key facts - **What**: Significant recovery in Swiss exports after months of stagnation - When: July 2026 - Where: Switzerland (national territory) - Who: UDSC (Federal Office of Customs and Border Security) - Export amount: CHF 27.8 billion - Trade balance surplus: CHF 8.1 billion (new monthly record) - Pharmaceutical growth: +25% (+3.3 billion CHF)
### The July Recovery
Swiss exports rebounded sharply in July 2026. According to the Federal Office of Customs and Border Security (FOCS), sales abroad reached CHF 27.8 billion, an increase of 13.8% compared to June net of seasonal effects. In real terms, adjusted for price developments, growth was 10.7%.
This is the highest level since March 2025, thus signaling a clear reversal of the trend after months of substantial stagnation. The USDC points out that the trend in foreign sales is now showing an upward trend, confirming that the export cycle has reached a turning point.
At the same time, imports suffered a significant contraction. In July they fell by 4.5% to CHF 19.6 billion. In ### Interpretation of the upturn: the national economic context
July's acceleration represents a significant reversal in the Swiss economic cycle. After months of stagnation, exporting companies are regaining ground on global markets. For the national economy, this has direct implications: greater production activity, higher export volumes, and potential employment stability in sectors traditionally linked to international trade.
The central role of the pharmaceutical sector — historically one of the pillars of Swiss exports — confirms Switzerland's competitive capacity even in periods of macroeconomic uncertainty. Swiss pharmaceutical companies operate on a global scale and maintain strong positions, as evidenced by the 25% growth recorded in July.
### The gap between exports and imports
A particularly relevant aspect emerges from the contrast between export and import dynamics. While foreign sales rose by 13,8%, foreign purchases fell by 4,5%. This gap directly impacts the national trade balance, with the surplus reaching a new monthly peak at 8,1 billion francs.
Dynamics of this type can reflect different scenarios: a phase of consolidation of national production, lower dependence on raw material imports, or a contraction in domestic demand. The FOCBS points out that the evolution of the main sectors has shown a sideways trend since October 2025, which would suggest that July's rebound could represent a cyclical oscillation rather than a lasting structural trend reversal.
### Pharmaceuticals and watches: the spears of export
Pharmaceuticals continue to be the main driver of the Swiss exporting economic recovery. The 25% growth (+3,3 billion CHF) testifies to robust demand on global markets for medicines and related products. These sectors are characterized by high innovation intensity, qualified human capital, and the ability to maintain competitive margins even in times of global uncertainty.
Watches confirm another niche of Swiss excellence with growing exports. Machinery and electronic products, on the other hand, remain in a neutral zone, suggesting a differentiation in the economic cycles of various industrial segments. For those operating in the sector and monitoring national economic prospects, the [Swiss cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) largely depends on the trend of global economic competitiveness and the solidity of the trade balance.

## In a nutshell - Swiss exports +13.8% in July 2026 compared to the previous month (seasonally adjusted data) - Imports -4.5% in the same period - Record monthly trade balance: +8.1 billion CHF
## Key facts - **What**: Marked recovery of Swiss foreign trade after months of stagnation - When: July 2026 (official statement of August 20, 2026) - Where: Switzerland, national level - Who: Swiss Federal Administration - Exports: +13.8% in monthly variation (seasonally adjusted) - Imports: -4.5% in monthly variation (seasonally adjusted) - Trade balance surplus: +8.1 billion CHF (new monthly record) - Driving sector: Chemical-pharmaceutical
### Net rebound after the stagnation period
In July 2026, Swiss foreign trade experienced a very mixed development, but decidedly favourable overall. In seasonally adjusted terms, exports reached a net increase of 13.8 percent compared to the previous month, while at the same time imports suffered a decrease of 4.5 percent. This divergent dynamic between outbound and inbound trade flows produced a direct and positive effect on the trade balance, which reached a new monthly record of 8.1 billion Swiss francs.
The relevant aspect is that the official source explicitly reports a "recovery in exports after months of stagnation". This means that the period ### What does the recovery mean for the Swiss economy
The recovery of exports after months of stagnation represents a significant change in trend for the Swiss economy as a whole. A 13.8 percent increase in monthly variation, even after seasonal adjustment, indicates a more vibrant international demand for Swiss products. At the same time, the 4.5 percent contraction in imports signals an asymmetric evolution: foreign markets are pulling more strongly towards Swiss goods, while domestic demand for imported goods is decreasing. This favorable imbalance directly generates a record trade surplus, which represents a valuable source of currency for the Swiss economic system and has a positive impact on foreign accounts.
### Implications for the Swiss franc exchange rate
A consistent trade surplus traditionally exercises upward pressure on the national currency. In the Swiss case, the July surplus of 8.1 billion francs may contribute to a progressive strengthening of the CHF against major currencies, including the EUR. For border residents who earn in euros and spend in Swiss francs, a stronger franc means a reduction in purchasing power in daily purchases, rents, healthcare expenses, and Swiss services in the medium to long term. Those who maintain euro savings suffer similarly from a relative loss of value in the exchange rate.
To monitor these effects, it is useful to regularly consult the data on the CHF/EUR exchange rate and official economic indicators published by UST/BFS.
### The pharmaceutical-chemical sector as the driving force of the recovery
The fact that the pharmaceutical-chemical sector is the main driver of both exports and imports in July 2026 highlights the central role that this sector plays in the Swiss economy. It is one of the pillars of the Swiss industrial system, characterized by massive investments in research and development, the production of high-tech pharmaceuticals with a very high technological content, and a sophisticated global network of suppliers and customers. The recovery in this sector is indicative of a renewed dynamics in international trade of high-tech and high-value-added products.
For those working in Switzerland, especially in the industrial and pharmaceutical-chemical sectors, the July commercial recovery represents a positive signal of occupational stability and potential growth in the following quarters. However, a single monthly data point does not allow us to affirm that the trend is definitively reversed: it will be necessary to monitor the subsequent data (August, September, October) to assess the sustainability of the recovery and to understand if it will extend to other sectors beyond the pharmaceutical-chemical sector.

A central element for obtaining the B permit is the availability of a verified job offer. This means that you generally need to have an employment contract or a promise of employment from an employer located in the canton (or Switzerland in general). If you believe you are eligible for a reduction, here are the steps to make a claim in the Canton of Schaffhausen:
1. **Document Preparation**: Collect your latest tax return, pay stubs for the past few months, family composition certificate (if you have children), and any documents for other income (pension, benefits, rent). If you are married or in a domestic partnership, you will need both partners' data.
2. Administrative Contacts: Visit the website of the Schaffhausen cantonal administration or call the competent office (usually the Health Office or Department of Health) to receive the official application form. The form is usually available online in PDF format.
3. Form Completion: Fill out the form with your personal data, health insurance number, annual gross and net income, number of dependents, and financial situation. Be accurate: errors in the data may delay processing or result in rejection.
4. Attachments: Add a copy of your previous year's tax return, current pay stubs, birth certificate of children (if not already registered), and a certificate of unemployment (if unemployed). If you are a pensioner, add a pension certificate.

If the administration denies the reduction because your income exceeds the limit, you have the right to contest the decision. You must file a complaint within 30 days of notification. ## In a nutshell - Maximum deposit of 3 months' rent, linked to an account in the name of the tenant - Lessor cancellation valid only on official cantonal form - Dispute fee within 30 days to the conciliation authority - Equal federal law in all Swiss cantons
## Key facts - **Regulation**: Civil Code (CO) articles 253 et seq. - Scope: Residential property lease agreements - Maximum deposit: 3 months of monthly rent - Dispute deadline: 30 days from receipt of fee notification - Application: Swiss federal law, identical in Basel-Country and in all cantons
Those who rent an apartment in Basel Campagna operate within the framework of a single federal law, identical everywhere in Switzerland. The Swiss Civil Code, articles 253 et seq., regulate residential property leases with uniform protections for tenants and landlords, from the French-speaking Switzerland to the cantons of German-speaking Switzerland up to Ticino. This uniformity guarantees legal certainty: a contract stipulated in Basel Campagna follows the same rules as in Zurich, Geneva or Lugano. Three central elements - the security deposit, the cancellation procedure, the challenge of the rent - are precisely regulated, protecting tenants from abuse and offering the owner clarity on deadlines.
### The security deposit: legal limits and tenant protection
The security deposit is one of the most delicate steps ### Legal terms for the termination of the contract
The termination of the lease follows strict deadlines set at the federal level. In the first year of the lease, the landlord (as well as the tenant) may terminate the lease with one month's notice; from the second to the ninth year of the current lease, the notice increases to two months; from the tenth year of the lease onwards, the landlord must comply with a three-month term. However, the procedure is not limited to the simple counting of days: the cancellation must be sent in writing using only the official cantonal form recognized by the Basel Countryside authorities, signed and dated correctly. Informal communication by email, telephone or instant message does not constitute a valid termination. In addition, the end of the month deadline (usually the 15th or last day of the calendar month) must be scrupulously observed. If the landlord does not comply with these formalities, the tenant may dispute the cancellation with the conciliation authority.
### Dispute of the initial fee and recourse to the conciliation authority
If the landlord proposes a rent deemed disproportionate to the local market prices, the tenant has a specific legal instrument. Under Swiss federal law, the tenant may challenge an initial fee if he considers that it is excessively high compared to what is practiced in Basel Countryside for
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Step-by-Step Procedure to Contest a Rent Amount
Phase 1: Receive and Document the Notice When the landlord communicates the proposed rent amount, they must send the notice in writing via registered letter or direct delivery. It is essential to preserve the document with the receipt date clearly indicated: this date marks the beginning of the 30-day period to take action.
Phase 2: Gather Market Data Before appealing to the authority, the tenant should document the rental amounts charged in Basel-Landschaft for comparable apartments. Square footage, geographical location (proximity to transportation), number of rooms, and amenities (cellar, garage, elevator) are determining factors. This documentation will support the challenge before the conciliation authority.
Phase 3: Submit the Appeal to the Conciliation Authority Within 30 days of receipt, the tenant submits a written appeal to the cantonal conciliation authority in Basel-Landschaft, attaching a copy of the rent notice and market documentation. In the appeal, they must clearly explain why they believe the rent amount is unjustifiably high.
Phase 4: Participation in the Conciliation Procedure The authority convenes the landlord and tenant for a joint conciliation meeting. Both parties present their arguments. The authority may order an appraisal of local market prices, especially if the parties' positions are far apart.
**Phase 5: Binding Decision** If conciliation fails, the authority issues a written decision binding on both parties. This decision establishes the fair rent amount according to market parameters.
### Key Deadlines and Documents to Keep
Always keep in paper or digital format: - Signed copy of the rental lease contract - Receipts for deposit payment (with date and amount) - All official correspondence from the landlord, preferably via registered mail - Photographic and video documentation of the apartment's condition upon entry - Copy of any lease termination notice received from the landlord - Documentation of expenses incurred for repairs (if relevant to future disputes)

item.title: Apprenticeship in Switzerland: contracts, salary and maturity
item.description: Internship contracts, remuneration, compulsory contributions and professional maturity: an apprenticeship guide in the Swiss training system.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Apprenticeship lasts 3-4 years and combines practical work and school education - AVS/AI contributions: 5.3% for the apprentice (10.6% for employer) - Minimum holidays: 4 weeks (5 under 20 years old) - Federal contract: the same rights in every Swiss canton
## Key facts - **What**: Dual education system that alternates practical work and vocational school - Where: All Swiss cantons, including Basel-Landschaft - Who: Young people from 15 years old and up - Duration: 3-4 years depending on the professional field - Mandatory contributions: AVS/AI 5.3% (employee), 10.6% (employer) - Maximum hours: 45 hours/week (industry, offices, sales) or 50 in other sectors
Apprenticeship is the heart of the Swiss vocational education system. It represents a path combining education and work: the student spends approximately 3-4 days a week in the company and one-two days in vocational school. In the canton of Basel-Landschaft, as in other cantons, the system follows uniform federal rules that define rights, duties and protections for anyone undertaking this path.
The apprenticeship contract is the fundamental document. Regulated by federal law, it must contain the company's data, the apprentice's details, the professional sector, the start date, the total duration, the weekly hours and the remuneration. Once signed by the company and apprentice (with parents or whoever exercises parental authority, if a minor), the contract acquires legal validity.
Working hours must not exceed 45 hours per week in industry, offices and sales, or 50 hours in other sectors. The apprentice is entitled to a minimum of 4 weeks of annual holidays — 5 weeks if under 20. These protections are guaranteed by federal law and apply uniformly in all cantons.
### How the remuneration system works
The apprentice's remuneration is established in the apprenticeship contract. There is no federal minimum wage, although many cantons have defined regional ones and several sectors have collective agreements. During the salary, the apprentice automatically pays 5.3% of AVS/AI contributions (the employer adds 10.6% to their account). Additionally, 1.1% up to the annual limit goes to unemployment insurance (UIC/UCA).
Accident insurance (LAINF/LAI) ranges between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the sector of activity and is covered by the employer. The LPP pension system (second pillar) usually does not apply to apprentices, as the remuneration is often below the coordination threshold. With the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) online it is possible to estimate net and charges on a hypothetical remuneration. ### Rights and protections during training
The traineeship contract must be filed with the competent cantonal office — in the canton of Basel-Country with the Vocational Training Office. The apprentice always receives a signed copy of the contract. If during the probationary period (usually 1-3 months) incompatibilities arise between the young person and the employer, the contract may be terminated with 1 week's notice by both parties.
After the probationary period, cancellation times are tightened: 1 month in the first year of apprenticeship, 2 months from the second to the ninth year, 3 months from the tenth year onwards. These times are established by federal law and apply in each canton.
Social contributions represent an important voice for those who hire an apprentice. On the one hand, the young person sees 5.3% of AVS/AI and 1.1% of AD/AC deducted from his net; on the other, the employer pays 10.6% of AVS/AI, 1.1% of AD/AC and the cost of LAINF/LAA accident insurance (0.7%-1.5% depending on the sector). All these payments are mandatory by federal law and identical in each canton.
### Health insurance and taxes
Health insurance (LAMal/KVG) is mandatory for anyone residing in Switzerland. The apprentice must stipulate it within 3 months of the start of the training. Premiums are determined by canton and tariff region; the canton Basel-Country has its own tariffs. Adult deductibles range from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 depending on plan
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Professional Maturity: Additional Qualification
Professional maturity is an additional qualification that apprentices can obtain in parallel with their apprenticeship or immediately after its conclusion. It consists of theoretical lessons in general subjects — languages, mathematics, history, economics, sciences — along with the practical training in the company. At the end of the apprenticeship, the young person obtains both the certificate of competence (AFC, federal apprenticeship diploma) and, if they have attended the mandatory courses, the professional maturity certificate.
Professional maturity is recognized at the federal level and is a privileged gateway to access professional university schools (SUP). Many cantons, including Basel-Landschaft, offer maturity courses at ordinary professional schools. The cost is usually free or minimal for the apprentice; the school is financed by the canton itself. Completing professional maturity simultaneously with the apprenticeship requires organization, but allows for further qualification without extending the overall training time.
### How to Find and Start an Apprenticeship
Searching for an apprenticeship position takes place mainly through national and regional job advertisement portals, the local employment office, direct contacts with companies in the field of interest, and school orientation fairs. Once a potential employer is found, the negotiation of the apprenticeship contract proceeds.
Before signing, it is essential to verify that the document contains: the name and address of the company, the name and date of birth of the apprentice, the professional branch, start date, total duration in years, declared weekly hours, monthly or annual remuneration and payment methods. The cantonal professional education office of Basel-Landschaft can provide advice on contractual standards and minimum rights.
### Next Steps
To navigate the world of apprenticeships and estimate your net salary after contributions and taxes, use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator). To search for apprenticeship offers in the canton of Basel-Landschaft, access specialized [job board](nav:jobs) portals, which allow you to filter by region, sector, and type of training. If you have questions about contracts, rights, hours, or contributions during the apprenticeship, the cantonal professional education office remains the main reference.

The decision concerns in particular the declaration and authorisation forms governed by Article 21 of the Ordinance instituting measures against the Islamic Republic of Iran.

These are not only companies that trade with the country, but also individual Swiss citizens who maintain financial relations abroad or who must transfer capital to family members or beneficiaries in Iran. Non-profit organizations and entities with offices in Switzerland also fall within the scope of the law.

Credit institutions will have the task of checking the compliance of the documentation and rejecting any requests based on obsolete forms. This could result in slower processing times during the first transition period.
### Prevent administrative errors The nature of the change makes it essential to acquire the correct forms promptly. For those working in the Canton of Basel-City, the gross salary indicated in a contract is subject to compulsory reductions due to social contributions. These are not taxes in the traditional sense, but funding for social protection systems run by federal agencies.
The ** AVS/AI system ** (Old Age and Survivors Insurance/Disability Insurance) is the first pillar of Swiss social security. Employees and employers each pay 5.3% of gross salary to these schemes. Unemployment insurance (AD) and occupational accident insurance (AC) add an additional 1.1% up to an annual cap. Non-occupational accident insurance (LAINF) varies from 0.7 to 1.5% depending on the sector of activity.
The second pillar, occupational pension (LPP — Law on occupational pension for old age, survivors and disability), is mandatory for those who earn above a minimum coordination threshold. However, it’s advisable to verify within the first weeks that the AVS number has been assigned and contributions have started. While federal law provides for 1/2/3 months’ notice based on seniority, individual contracts might include longer or shorter terms (usually longer). Doing so from the first day of employment avoids surprises and ensures legal protection.

item.description: How Swiss wages work by level of training, compulsory social contributions, collective agreements and cantonal minimum wage.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - AVS/AI/IPG contributions amount to 5.3% for the employee (10.6% with the employer) - The maximum hours are 45 hours per week in industry, offices and sales; 50 in other sectors - The LPP provides for pension contributions from 7% to 18% of the coordinated salary according to age - Some cantons have their own minimum wage; Switzerland has no federal minimum
## Key facts - **What**: Compulsory wage structure and social security contributions in Switzerland - Who: Employees, employers, Federal Office of Social Security (UFAS/BSV) - Where: Entire Swiss territory (national + cantonal regulations) - When: Continuous application; amounts indexed annually - AVS contribution: 5.3% employee + 5.3% employer (total 10.6%) - LPP age 25-34: Minimum 7% of the coordinated salary
The Swiss labour market is based on a wage structure that is strictly regulated at federal and cantonal level. Those who work in Switzerland automatically pay mandatory contributions for old-age and survivors' insurance (AVS), disability insurance (AI) and unemployment insurance (IPG). These three contributions amount to 5.3% of the gross salary for the employee, while the employer pays an identical share, for a total of 10.6%.
To these are added contributions for family allowances (variable amount according to the canton), accident insurance (LAINF/LAA, between 0.7% and 1.5% according to the sector of ## Training, qualifications and salary levels
In Switzerland, the link between level of education and salary level is direct. Those who have an apprenticeship certification (initial vocational training, AFC) have access to different salary levels than those who have completed high school, and still different from those who have graduated from a university or polytechnic school. However, the SOURCE CONTENT does not specify precise minimum wage figures by degree of training, because the Swiss system does not have a single national minimum wage.
### Minimum Wage: Federal Absence and Cantonal Diversity
Unlike many European countries, Switzerland does not have a federal law setting a national minimum wage. This means that the minimum wage protection is managed by the individual cantons and, in some cases, by collective labour agreements (CCLs). Some cantons have introduced their own cantonal minimum wages; others rely entirely on collective agreements and the market. For those who work or are looking for a job in Switzerland, it is therefore essential to check the regulations of the canton of residence or employment.
Collective labour agreements play a central role in determining wages and conditions of employment. These agreements are negotiated between trade unions (on the one hand) and employers' associations (on the other) and set minimum wages, wage increases, working hours, public holidays and additional benefits for entire sectors
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## How to navigate the Swiss salary system: concrete actions
Anyone starting a job in Switzerland or already working and looking to negotiate a promotion needs to understand the practical workings of the salary package. A typical Swiss salary package shows:
1. **Gross salary**: the amount agreed upon in the employment contract 2. Deductions (AVS/AI/IPG 5.3%, LPP according to age and coordination, LAINF/LAA 0.7-1.5%, VAT if due, any salary tax) 3. Net salary: what remains after all deductions
To verify the accuracy of your salary package, it's a good idea to consult the applicable rates in your canton and industry. The SECO (State Secretariat for Economic Affairs) and the cantonal offices of social security provide free online calculators.
### Step 1: Check the cantonal minimum salary
Before negotiating or accepting a job offer, check the cantonal administration website to see if there is a minimum salary in your canton. If not, consult the applicable collective labor agreement (available on union or employer association websites).
### Step 2: Calculate the coordinated salary for LPP
The coordinated salary is not the gross salary, but a technical concept: gross salary minus a fixed deduction (the amount of which is adjusted annually). From this coordinated salary, the pension contributions are deducted according to your age group. Use the pension funds' or your employer's online calculators to get precise estimates.
### Step 3: Collective labor agreements and salary protection
If your industry has a collective labor agreement, read it carefully to see what benefits are included, such as annual pay increases, performance bonuses, 13th month, sick leave benefits, and other non-visible benefits in the basic salary. Unions and employer associations provide free consultations on the correct application of collective labor agreements.
### Step 4: Plan the third pillar (third pillar 3a)
In addition to AVS/AHV (first pillar) and LPP/BVG (second pillar), Swiss workers can voluntarily contribute to a [third pillar 3a](nav:pillar3) for supplementary pension savings with tax benefits. The maximum amount that can be contributed is adjusted annually and is different for employees with or without LPP.
## Practical implications: what to check before signing
Before signing a contract, make sure you:
- Know your monthly or annual gross salary and check that it is equal to or higher than the cantonal minimum (if it exists) - Understand which pension fund manages LPP and what rate will be applied - Check if your contract is covered by a collective labor agreement - Check the estimated net salary using an online calculator - Inform yourself about the statutory notice period if you want to terminate the employment relationship in the future
The Swiss labor market protects employees through central and standardized federal regulations, as well as cantonal and union-level negotiations. Understanding these rules means protecting yourself and negotiating your contract consciously.

## In a nutshell - The compensation fund manages AVS contributions (5.3% employees, 10.6% total with employer) - Contribution gaps reduce future income by as much as 1-2% per missing year - Complementary services fill the gap between income and cantonal minimum wage

## First pillar and cantonal compensation fund
The cantonal compensation fund of the Canton of Basel-City is the entity responsible for the concrete management of the first pillar of social security, namely Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance (AVS). It is not a personal savings fund, but a solidarity contribution system: those who work pay AVS contributions (5.3% for employees, 10.6% total with the employer's contribution) that directly finance the pensions of current pensioners.
The fund collects these contributions through the salary and pays them to the Confederation, which then redistributes the funds to the cantonal funds on the basis of demographic needs and income demands. At the same time, the cantonal fund calculates and pays old-age, survivors' and ## Complementary services and minimum life expectancy in the canton
When the AVS annuity is not sufficient to cover the cost of living, supplementary benefits (PC) intervene. In the Canton of Basel-City, supplementary benefits are provided by the Department of Health and Social Affairs (DSS) in coordination with the cantonal compensation fund.
Supplementary benefits are not a charitable welfare measure, but a right enshrined in the Federal Act on Supplementary Benefits to AVH and AI (LPPC). Any resident who reaches retirement age and does not have sufficient income can make use of it.
### The concept of vital minimum
PCs calculate the difference between disposable income (AVS income + other income from work, rent or property, private pensions, AI annuities) and the ** living minimum ** recognized in the canton. The living minimum covers rent, food, energy, communications, local transport and essential needs.
In 2026, the reference federal minimum wage remains indexed annually according to the SVP (Business Statistics) wage index. Each canton may set slightly different amounts based on the local cost of living. In the Canton of Basel-City, the living minimum is established by the State Council and communicated annually through the administrative circulars.

Those living in the City of Basel and approaching retirement age must follow a precise procedure to ensure they do not lose money owed and obtain the optimal combination of AVS and PC. Here are the concrete steps.
### Step 1: Request an Individual Account (Versichertenkonto)
At least 4–6 months before the scheduled retirement date, contact the cantonal compensation fund of the City of Basel to request your individual account (Versichertenkonto / Dossier individuel). This document summarizes:
- All contributions paid since the first job to date - Any gaps and non-covered periods - The average income calculated according to the federal formula
The request is free and can be made online, by mail, or in person at the counter. The fund will send the account within 2–3 weeks.
### Step 2: Verify and Fill Gaps in Contributions
By examining the account, identify any gaps. If present and dating back to the last 5 years, it is possible to pay voluntary retroactive contributions. The fund provides an estimate of the amount due.
For periods of indemnified unemployment, the unemployment insurance (AD/AC) automatically covers contributions, so no manual intervention is required.
For other missing periods (periods abroad, non-indemnified illness), retroactive payment is optional but highly recommended: each year filled increases the future pension by approximately 2–2.5%.
### Step 3: Obtain the Pension Simulation
The cantonal compensation fund provides a written simulation of the estimated AVS pension based on current data. This document indicates:
- The gross monthly pension amount - Deductions (LAMal contributions, if applicable) - The effective net amount
The simulation is binding for the fund; it allows for planning the pension budget and evaluating whether it will be necessary to apply for PC.
### Step 4: Submit a Request for Supplementary Benefits (if necessary)
If the simulated pension does not reach the cantonal minimum, submit a request for PC by the month in which the retirement age is reached. The request must be filed with the PC office of the City of Basel (Department of Health and Social Affairs, DSS).
Required documentation:
- Lease agreement and payment receipts (last 3 months) - Income tax declaration (last 2 fiscal years) - Bank statement extracts (last 2 months) - Property certificate (if owner-occupied) - Active LAMal policy for each family member - Certificate of absence of significant assets (if required)
### Step 5: Follow the Liquidation
The cantonal compensation fund liquidates the AVS pension from the first day of the month following the retirement age (or the chosen date if it is postponed). The amount is paid monthly to a designated bank account.
The PC office communicates the decision on the request for supplementary benefits within 30–45 days. If approved, the PC is paid simultaneously with the AVS pension.
### Free Support and Counseling
The cantonal compensation fund of the City of Basel offers completely free counseling throughout all stages. It is possible to contact the office by phone, email, or in person. Many funds also provide digital counseling and downloadable information material online.
Alternative: the SVP (Voluntary Service for Pensioners) counters in many municipalities offer free voluntary assistance with filling out forms and preparing the application.
For those who want to deepen the pension calculation and understand the AVS/PC system better, it is possible to use the [federal AVS calculator](nav:pension) available on the UFAS/BSV website. For tax-related issues related to the pension, consult the cantonal tax administration of the City of Basel.

item.description: Since 2016, the Federal Council has automatically incorporated the UN sanctions lists into Swiss law. SESAM update of 19 August 2026.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell
- On 19.08.2026 the SESAM database was updated with the new UN sanctions list - Since 2016, the Federal Council has automatically incorporated UN measures - The changes acquire immediate legal validity in Switzerland - SESAM is the federal tool for verifying compliance with sanctions
## Key facts
- **What**: Automatic updating of UN sanctions lists in the Swiss SESAM database - When: 19 August 2026 (update); 4 March 2016 (ordinance) - Where: Swiss Federal SESAM System - Who: Federal Council and UN Security Council - Legal basis: Ordinance on the automatic transposition of UN sanctions lists
On August 19, 2026, the Federal Council communicated an update relevant to anyone conducting international economic operations. The SESAM database, the Swiss Federal Sanctions Management System, has been updated to reflect the changes made by the UN Sanctions Committee to the lists of individuals, businesses and organisations subject to restrictive measures. An event that might seem purely technical, but which has concrete implications for millions of transactions involving Switzerland.
This update is not an isolated event. It represents the application of a structural decision of the Federal Council dated 4 March 2016. On that date, the Swiss Executive approved an order establishing the automatic transposition of the lists of ### Who is subject to verification obligations
The network of Swiss subjects who have to check the SESAM database before making international transactions is much wider than you might imagine. It's not just about ** financial institutions ** and large multinationals. Anyone in Switzerland who transfers funds abroad, receives international payments, imports goods or participates in commercial transactions abroad enters a potential risk zone if they do not verify the counterparty in the SESAM list.
This includes [aziende piccole e medie](nav:companies), professionals (consultants, accountants, lawyers), traders, real estate entrepreneurs negotiating with foreign clients. Individuals who, for example, receive an international wire transfer or intend to invest funds abroad should also be aware that their contractor could appear on the list and make the transaction illegal.
Swiss banks and financial institutions, in particular, carry out systematic and automatic checks. Their systems are connected to SESAM and verify every transaction in real time. When the list is updated, such as August 19, 2026, these systems adjust immediately without manual intervention.
### Implications of Automatic Compliance
The immediate incorporation of UN sanctions into Swiss law has a fundamental practical consequence: there is no room for “I didn't know” or “I hadn't seen the update yet”. From the moment in which the
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How to access and consult SESAM
The SESAM database is publicly accessible on the Federal Administration website. The database allows you to search for names of natural persons, business names of enterprises, names of organizations and entities to verify whether they appear in the official list of UN sanctions incorporated into Swiss law. Access is free and does not require registration; anyone can consult it from any internet-connected device.
To perform a search, you need to enter the name (or part of it) of the counterparty. The system returns results by homonymy, so it is advisable to refine the search with additional details: date of birth, place of origin, sector of activity or identification number. SESAM is available in multilingual versions (German, French, Italian, English), facilitating access to non-native speakers as well.
If the search returns a result that matches the counterparty, you must immediately refrain from the transaction. In case of doubt — when the name is very similar but not identical — it is prudent to contact the competent Office of the Federal Administration (which manages SESAM) for clarification. Proceeding without certainty exposes you to legal liability.
### Monitoring and ongoing compliance
Compliance with UN sanctions is not a one-off burden, but a continuous one. For those managing long-term commercial relations with foreign counterparties, it is advisable to implement a structured practice: check SESAM initially before starting the relationship, monitor periodically (quarterly or at least annually) whether the counterparty remains compliant by re-entering the name in the database, maintain documentary record of these checks (useful in case of disputes), and activate automatic alerts or monitoring services if your company operates in high-risk sectors.
For companies operating in areas such as import/export, international financial services or commercial intermediation, systematic monitoring is now standard practice, often integrated into due diligence processes. ## In a nutshell - A carpenter in the Canton of Zurich sought a secretary "preferably non-smoker, between 22 and 40 years old" - The announcement sparked an online debate: those who felt excluded protested - A labor law expert confirms that the ad is admissible under federal law
## Key facts - **What**: Job advertisement with criteria of gender, age and smoking habits - When: August 2026 - Where: Canton Zurich (Switzerland) - Who: Carpentry + Prof. Roger Rudolph (University of Zurich, labour law) - Applicable rule: Federal Law on Gender Equality (LPar) - Maximum allowance: Three monthly salary payments
### The case of Zurich carpentry
A carpenter's shop in the canton of Zurich has published a job advertisement for an administrative secretary who immediately ignited the online debate. The requirements were specific: "Preferably non-smoker, age about 22-40 years". In addition, due to the “already predominant male presence” in the team, a female person was desired.
The announcement drew criticism especially among those who felt excluded beforehand: men and smokers protested on social networks. Contacted by 20 Minuten, the carpenter chose not to make public statements. The question that many have asked themselves was immediate: to what extent is it legal to ask for such specific characteristics in a Swiss job advertisement?
### The assessment ### When discrimination is triggered in the hiring phase
According to Professor Rudolph, if a man applies despite the indication of preference for the female gender and is rejected solely because of his sex, this could constitute discrimination under the LPar. The detail about the male prevalence of the team does not fundamentally change the issue from a legal point of view. It is possible to publish an advertisement addressed to a woman, but once the application of a man has been received, the evaluation must be based on objective criteria of merit, not on gender.
“If sex alone is the reason for exclusion, then it would most likely be discrimination,” Rudolph explained. This principle is central to the protection offered by LPar to Swiss workers.
### The maximum compensation provided by law
Individuals who experience gender discrimination during the hiring process may be able to seek legal compensation. The maximum amount is three monthly salary payments. An important detail: there is no right to get the job. The ruling or recognition of discrimination does not imply an obligation for the company to hire the discriminated candidate, but only to pay financial compensation.

If a candidate believes they have been discriminated against on the basis of gender during the hiring process, they have the opportunity to take action to protect their rights. The first step is to carefully document every communication received from the company and gather evidence demonstrating the reason for the discrimination. Once the evidence has been collected, the candidate may consider filing a complaint with the competent authorities or consulting with a labor law professional to evaluate the available options.
It is important to act promptly, as legal actions are subject to specific deadlines. A legal consultant or attorney specializing in labor law can provide precise guidance on the timeframe for filing an appeal and on the competent jurisdiction.
### Practical Implications for Employers and Candidates
This case involving the Zurich carpentry firm offers an important lesson for all Swiss companies publishing job advertisements. While the law allows for a certain flexibility in the wording of job ads and in the search for specific profiles, employers must be careful not to discriminate against candidates who apply during the evaluation phase.
For candidates, the lesson is equally relevant: if they believe they are discriminated against during the hiring process for reasons protected by federal law (particularly gender), they have legal remedies available. The maximum compensation of three months' salary represents a tangible remedy, even if it does not restore the lost opportunity to obtain the job.
### What Does 'LPar' Protection Really Mean
The Federal Gender Equality Act does not prohibit job advertisements from specifying gender preferences, as confirmed by Rudolph. However, protection kicks in when applications are being evaluated. A company cannot legitimately reject a candidate solely based on gender if they meet the required professional qualifications.
Protection regarding age and other factors remains less defined and more difficult to enforce in a hiring context. ## In brief - 2026 budget surplus: +0.8 billion CHF (vs projected deficit of -0.7 billion) - Corporate income tax revenue: +1.4 billion, concentrated in Lucerne, Zurich, Basel and Geneva - Additional military spending credit: 970 million CHF for air defence and drone protection
## Key facts - **What**: First projection of the Confederation's 2026 budget - When: 19 August 2026 (communication to the Federal Council) - Where: Swiss Confederation - Who: Federal Council - Surplus: 0.8 billion CHF (instead of projected deficit of 0.7 billion) - Revenue increase: +1.9 billion adjusted in June - SNB: Profit distribution +0.3 billion beyond budget
On 19 August 2026, the Federal Council communicated the first projection of the federal budget for the current year. The result is surprisingly positive: the Confederation expects a financing surplus of just under 0.8 billion francs, whereas the initial budget projected a deficit of approximately 0.7 billion. This turnaround is mainly driven by growth in revenue from corporate income tax, which had already emerged in early summer based on data from the Cantons and could therefore be taken into account in the 2027 budget.
The improvement was recorded in the ordinary budget, where estimated revenues were revised upwards by 1.9 billion in June. However, the projection also includes an additional credit of 970 million intended for additional military spending — resources needed for air defence systems and protection against mini drones. This increased spending means that ordinary expenditures will also exceed the budgeted amount by 0.8 billion.
### Ordinary and extraordinary budget
In the extraordinary budget, the Confederation benefits from higher revenues from the profit distribution of the Swiss National Bank (SNB), which is 0.3 billion higher than budgeted. In contrast, extraordinary expenditures remain stable at 470 million, corresponding to contributions scheduled for the Cantons to accommodate persons seeking protection from Ukraine. If you wish to understand how your federal tax burden is positioned within the Swiss tax structure, you can use the [federal tax calculator](nav:calculator). According to the Parliament Act (LParl; RS 171.10), the Federal Council is required to carry out two approximate calculations of the expected result of the financial year each year by 30 June and 30 September. The projection is an estimate and should therefore be interpreted with caution, as unforeseen economic situations may alter the final results. ## Corporate Tax Revenues Drive the Budget
The most significant increase concerns corporate income tax, which has risen by 1.4 billion compared to the previous estimate. This growth is concentrated in specific Cantons: Lucerne, Zurich, and Basel-Stadt recorded revenues significantly higher than expected, a phenomenon attributable to a limited number of particularly profitable companies. Geneva, for its part, generated additional temporary revenues from both corporate income tax (+0.2 billion) and income tax (+0.2 billion), added to the 1.2 billion one-off amounts already included in the initial budget, following a review of the cantonal situation in light of the previous year's data.
Beyond corporate income tax, the Confederation also benefits from higher-than-expected revenues from mineral oil tax, with an increase of 0.3 billion. This increase is due to a less pronounced than expected evolution in the spread of electric vehicles, which slows the contraction of revenue from traditional fuels. The overall picture of ordinary revenues thus shows a diversification of positive sources, not limited to corporate profits alone.
### Implications for Taxpayers and Cantons
A positive projection of the federal budget has tangible effects on the Confederation's capacity to finance its competencies and transfer resources to the Cantons. The surplus of 0.8 billion CHF allows greater flexibility in spending decisions, although the additional credit of 970 million for armament absorbs a significant portion of this margin. The decision to invest in air defense and drone protection reflects the Confederation's foreign policy and security priorities in an evolving geopolitical context.
For Swiss taxpayers, the positive performance of corporate income tax is an indicator of the economic health of certain regions and sectors, but it does not necessarily translate into tax reductions at the federal level, since fiscal policy decisions remain the prerogative of Parliament and the Federal Council. The Federal Council announced on 19 August 2026 a decision destined to revolutionise the wheeled delivery industry in Switzerland. Electric commercial vehicles up to 4.25 tons will receive the same regulatory treatment as traditional vans, breaking down a series of administrative constraints that until now hindered the competitiveness of green mobility in national freight transport.
The decision stems from the examination of the results of the consultation and involves the amendment of as many as five federal ordinances on road traffic. The stated objective is twofold: to pave the way for the spread of electric mobility in the sector and to accelerate the decarbonisation of the delivery sector, a strategic priority for the Confederation in the framework of the transition ### Economic impact on national logistics
Equalization represents a concrete economic catalyst for delivery companies evaluating investments in electric fleets. Until now, a 4-tonne electric van remained subject to heavy vehicle rules: mandatory tachograph, motorway speed restrictions, and driving time constraints. These administrative burdens eroded the margins of ecological and economic advantage compared to traditional combustion models, discouraging the transition even for companies sensitive to sustainability.
With the new legislation entering into force on October 1, 2026, the calculation of operating costs changes radically. A driver of an equalized electric van will be able to:
- Save travel time on long motorway stretches, thanks to the permitted 120 km/h (vs. 100 km/h for traditional heavy vans) - Avoid daily tachograph completion and associated administrative compliance costs - Benefit from less frequent technical maintenance cycles, shortening vehicle downtime - Operate with greater schedule flexibility, thanks to exemptions from work and rest time constraints
These considerations directly affect the profitability of delivery services, especially for couriers and small [logistics companies](nav:companies) operating on repeated national routes (e.g., same-day deliveries from a distribution center to distant cities).
